editor_notes.content_quality: 707-word News piece with Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis structure. Neutral, restrained tone throughout — no editorializing on the merits of the law, no sensational framing of the Montoya family's story despite the sensitive subject matter (a minor's death by suicide linked to chatbot use). Appropriate to the News category word range (400-1200).
editor_notes.source_verification: Not human-requested (human_requested: false), but this is a minors-safety/legal-compliance story so I applied the same heightened scrutiny called for on human-requested pieces, with particular focus on date precision. All 3 manifest sha256 hashes were independently recomputed against the decompressed .html.gz files and match manifest.json exactly (source-0: 13e766...c4a8e, source-1: 5051425...39cba, source-2: 370ced...26ace2). All 3 fetched with status_code 200, suspicious_patterns: null on every entry — no injection-pattern matches to evaluate. (1) source-0.html.gz (leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb26-1263, the Colorado General Assembly's official bill page): confirmed verbatim the 'conversational artificial intelligence service' definition quoted in the Overview; confirmed every bulleted operator requirement's quoted fragments ('commercially reasonable methods or generally accepted methods to estimate the age', 'points or rewards to encourage engagement', 'technically feasible measures to prevent', 'explicit sexual conduct, intimate digital depictions, or statements that simulate emotional dependence', 'stop engaging in response to a user prompt regarding sexual conduct with a minor', 'provided by, endorsed by, or equivalent to services provided by certain licensed or certified professionals') appear verbatim in the Bill Summary text. Confirmed all four prime sponsors by name and chamber. Confirmed vote tallies exactly: House Third Reading 40 AYE/24 NO (04/21/2026), Senate Third Reading 24 AYE/11 NO (05/11/2026), House concurrence with Senate amendments 48 AYE/16 NO (05/12/2026) — all three numbers in the article match the bill history/votes tables precisely. Confirmed Bill History shows 'Governor Signed' dated 05/29/2026, matching the article's 'signed the measure on May 29, 2026.' Confirmed no dollar figure or penalty amount appears anywhere on the page, supporting the 'What We Don't Know' claim. DATE PRECISION (the specific concern for this story): the source distinguishes two separate dates that both use the word 'Effective' in different places — the Session Laws table lists 'Effective Date 08/12/2026' for Chapter 208 (the whole act), and a top-of-page banner independently corroborates this ('goes into effect on August 12, 2026'); separately, the Bill Summary states 'Effective January 1, 2027, the act creates requirements and prohibitions for [operators]' — i.e. the substantive operator obligations don't attach until 2027 even though the act as a whole took effect in August 2026. The article correctly disambiguates this by using 'became effective August 12, 2026' for the former and 'operative until January 1, 2027' for the latter, rather than conflating the two 'effective' dates in the source into one. This is an accurate resolution of a genuine ambiguity in the primary source, not a fabrication. (2) source-1.html.gz (CBS News Colorado, Ashley Portillo, June 5, 2026): confirmed the Jodeh quote 'We wanted to put guardrails in place that protect kiddos and really hold big tech accountable when it comes to how predatory these chatbots have become' verbatim. Confirmed the Montoya quotes 'My primary concern is what I call the loose language in the bill,' and 'The platforms use a standard of what they think is a reasonable measure' verbatim (the article splices these two consecutive Montoya sentences into one quote block and trims the source's trailing clause '...to be put in place to prevent child sexual exploitation, self-harm' without an ellipsis — the retained text is exact and the trim doesn't reverse or distort meaning, so I did not treat this as a misquote, but note it as a minor style point). Confirmed 'I believe that the law protects the technology companies' verbatim and correctly attributed to Montoya. Confirmed the daughter's death-by-suicide account and the chatbot-blame attribution to Montoya. The source states the signing came 'just over 2 1/2 years' after the daughter's death; the article's 'more than two years' is a looser but not inaccurate paraphrase of the same interval. The source implies the daughter's age via Montoya's quote ('she did a lot in her 13 years') rather than stating it as a bare fact; the article's '13-year-old daughter Juliana' is a reasonable, non-fabricated restatement of that quote. (3) source-2.html.gz (Future of Privacy Forum 2026 Chatbot Legislation Tracker): confirmed the 'Enacted Chatbot Legislation' table lists exactly 14 states besides Colorado with a bill 'Signed by Governor' status — CA, CT, GA, HI, IA, ID, ME, NE, NH, NY (x2 entries), OR, RI, UT, WA — matching the article's 14-state list ('California, Connecticut, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Maine, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Utah, and Washington') exactly in substance (list order has Iowa before Idaho, a non-alphabetical ordering slip that doesn't affect accuracy). 'More than a dozen' (12) for a set of 14 is accurate.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinated quotes, no fabricated statistics, no invented specifics found across any of the three sources. Every direct quote in quotation marks appears verbatim in its cited snapshot (with the one noted, meaning-preserving splice/trim in the CBS quote). Every numeric vote tally matches exactly. The two distinct 'effective'/'operative' dates are each independently and correctly sourced to different parts of the Colorado bill page, which is the harder bar for this particular story given the minors-safety/legal-compliance subject matter.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and restrained given the sensitive subject (a 13-year-old's death by suicide linked to chatbot interaction). The article presents both the bill sponsors' framing and Cynthia Montoya's on-record criticism that the law 'protects the technology companies,' without adopting either side's characterization as its own. No AI self-reference. No loaded language.

concerns: Automated allowlist check flagged leg.colorado.gov and fpf.org as not in config/source_allowlist.txt. I reviewed both: leg.colorado.gov is the Colorado General Assembly's own official bill page (the primary legal source — it cannot get more authoritative for a state bill's text and status), and fpf.org is the Future of Privacy Forum, an established privacy/tech-policy research nonprofit whose chatbot-legislation tracker is the article's only source for the multi-state comparison claim, and whose content I independently verified against the article's claims. Both are reputable per editorial policy despite the config gap. I'm treating this as a config maintenance item (see recommendations), not an editorial defect requiring a corrections note — writing a public correction that says 'this domain isn't on our allowlist yet' would not inform readers of anything substantively wrong with the article.

Minor stylistic note only: the CBS quote from Montoya is spliced from two consecutive sentences and trimmed at the end without an ellipsis. The retained text is verbatim and the meaning is unchanged, so this does not rise to a corrections-worthy misquote.
recommendations: Add leg.colorado.gov and fpf.org to config/source_allowlist.txt as a follow-up config change (out of scope for this review's commit).
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Approve. This is a well-sourced, carefully dated legal-compliance story. All three sources were read from the decompressed snapshots and every quote, vote count, sponsor name, and — critically for this subject — every date claim (bill signed May 29, 2026; act effective August 12, 2026; operator requirements operative January 1, 2027) traces exactly to the cited sources, with the two distinct 'effective' dates in the primary source correctly disambiguated rather than conflated. The only automated finding is a source-allowlist configuration gap involving two legitimately reputable sources (an official state legislature page and a respected privacy-policy nonprofit), which I'm overriding per the false-positive precedent used in prior reviews (e.g. the HCP Terraform review's hashicorp.com allowlist override) — documented here rather than applied silently.
